metadata.detail:
DAVID, 2026-08-29: 'We have some protocol errors if we can't durably get these fixes to land.' He said it while blocked on design-doc packet c4b7c904, whose fix was ALREADY BUILT, GATED GREEN AND PARKED as car c6531868 — a car whose commit message names c4b7c904 explicitly. The fix existed and could not reach him.

WHY IT COULD NOT REACH HIM. Boarding is gated on DOCK DEPTH (min_dock_depth=4) or the twice-daily 06:05/18:05 clock. c6531868 sat parked and green while the dock held 3 boardable cars, so the queue-depth rule could not fire and the next clock window was ~90 minutes away. Nothing in the boarding decision knows that one of those cars unblocks a human and the other three do not. A car that ends someone's outage waits behind a batch-size rule designed for throughput.

(Compounded, but not caused, by the stale-ref defect fixed today as 212655bc: the conductor read the dock as 2 rather than 3. Even counted correctly it was below the threshold of 4, so the wait was real either way. Do not read this as a duplicate of that fix.)

THE FAST PATH EXISTS AND IS CLOSED TO THE ACTOR WHO FINDS THE BLOCK. `infra/push-step-plugins.sh` puts a step-plugin bundle on the cluster in about 46 seconds with no image build, no train and no pod roll — built for exactly this case (David, 2026-08-14: 'Since Step UX is just a javascript bundle, do we have a way to deploy those faster?'). This fix is a ONE-FILE, 34-line change to `infra/step-plugins/review-design.js` and nothing else in the train touches a bundle, so it is precisely the shape that path was made for. But the agent credential cannot use it:

    kubectl -n boss auth can-i get configmap     -> no
    kubectl -n boss auth can-i update configmap  -> no

`/etc/boss-dev/kubeconfig` is namespace-scoped to boss-dev. So the agent can diagnose the block, build the fix, gate it and park it — and then must hand the human a command to unblock himself. That is the protocol error: the mechanism built to unblock a person fast is unavailable to the actor who discovers the block, and the person it protects is the one it makes wait.

THREE CANDIDATE SHAPES, and the choice is a real design call, not an obvious fix:
  1. AN EXPEDITE MARK ON THE CAR. `metadata.expedite` (or a `blocks_person` edge naming the packet and person) makes the car board on the next tick regardless of dock depth. Cheapest, and it puts urgency in the protocol data where the rest of the operating model lives rather than in a human's judgement.
  2. GRANT THE BUNDLE PATH. A narrow RBAC rule letting the dev-session credential update ONLY the `step-plugins` ConfigMap in ns boss. Note the standing rule: this must land as a MANIFEST EDIT in infra/cluster/manifests/, not a kubectl apply, or it silently reverts on the next converge (the exact failure that removed the batch/jobs grant on 2026-08-28). Widens the agent's blast radius and deserves scrutiny on its own.
  3. ACCEPT THE WAIT, and make it honest: when a car names a packet that a person is blocked on, say so on the board and give an ETA, so the wait is visible rather than felt.

RECOMMENDATION: 1, with 3 as its rendering. It needs no new credential, keeps the cluster's declared state untouched, and is a rule change in the layer that is supposed to hold the operating model. 2 is a separate decision about how much the agent is trusted to apply directly, which is David's call and should not ride in on the back of an outage.

MEASURED COST THIS INSTANCE: fix parked and green before the block was reported; ~30-60 minutes to reach him by train (CI was 4/5 green with the slow `test` job outstanding at the time of filing); ~46 seconds by the path that exists. This is the second time this file's class of bug has blocked a design review live — 4f4f2f40 was the first, and its residual ('authoring should auto-populate') was never built either.

SAME CLASS AS aa783636, DIFFERENT VERB, and this one is worse because the wrong answer looks like success.

`boss docs` resolves its API as `std::env::var("BOSS_DOCS_API").unwrap_or_else(|| boss_ports::url("docs"))` (docs.rs:19-21), which on boss-gcp is the LOCAL 127.0.0.1:7050 — the legacy deployment, not the cluster that serves the Design Review page David reads.

MEASURED 2026-08-29, both instances live and both answering:

    LOCAL  127.0.0.1:7050        52 docs indexed,  0 queued flush jobs
    CLUSTER (via the gateway)    52 docs indexed,  3 queued flush jobs holding 11 decisions
                                                  30 failed jobs holding 135 decisions

So `boss docs flush-pending` run the documented way on boss-gcp finds an EMPTY queue, prints that there is nothing to flush, exits zero, and leaves eleven of David's recorded answers stuck on the cluster. A verb whose whole job is "apply the decisions" reporting success while applying none is the exact shape the doors rule in CLAUDE.md exists for: a wrong target answers instead of erroring.

The same applies to `boss docs reindex` — it would refresh the legacy index while the cluster's goes untouched.

WHY IT DRIFTED: the default was correct when BOSS ran on boss-gcp. The 2026-08-13 split-brain fix repointed JOB writes with BOSS_JOBS_URL drop-ins and left every other client on its old default. `boss gate` was the same defect and was fixed today (car ffe00199, backlog aa783636); this is the remaining sibling.

PROPOSED: the same first-choice option that packet took — NO default. Refuse without BOSS_DOCS_API and name the system of record in the error. Cheap, and it converts a silent no-op into a loud stop.

SECOND, AND IT IS THE REAL BLOCKER: even with the right address, the cluster's docs API is only reachable through the gateway, which needs a session — and the guest session the system issues is `audit-readonly`, so it can read the queue (which is how these numbers were measured) and cannot flush it. There is no machine door for docs writes the way boss-jobs-internal (10.20.0.34:7900) is one for jobs. Flushing the cluster's queue today needs either that door or a human session. Worth deciding alongside the address fix, because fixing only the default leaves the verb correctly refusing and still unable to do the work.

metadata.detail:
FOUND while draining the maintenance sweeps on 2026-08-29, and it is the sharpest instance of a pattern David asked me to watch for.

THE CLUSTER CONFORMANCE SWEEP CANNOT BE PERFORMED BY ITS ASSIGNEE. `infra/cluster/check-manifests-applied.sh` run with the only credential the agent has (/etc/boss-dev/kubeconfig, the namespace-scoped dev-session ServiceAccount) reports:

    check-manifests-applied: 2 present, 0 missing, 29 unreadable (of 31)
      29 of 31 objects were not readable by this credential, so this
      run verified 2. That is 'unknown', not 'clean'.

The script is well-built — it refuses to call its own result clean, which is why this was diagnosable at all. The problem is upstream of it: the daily sweep lands on an actor without the capability to answer the question.

THE ACCUMULATION IS THE PROOF. Of six daily sweep types, cluster-conformance is the ONLY one with three open packets (2026-08-27, 08-28, 08-29); the others had one or two. That difference is not attention, it is capability. A recurring obligation whose assignee cannot discharge it produces backlog at exactly the cadence rate, indefinitely, and looks identical to neglect.

THE GENERAL SHAPE, which is the part worth fixing. Nothing in the protocol expresses what a step NEEDS in order to be doable. Stations gate a claim on capability (`capability` is a column on the station registry and the claim CAS checks it), but a cadence-spawned sweep is not claimed through a station — it is created with a step that someone is expected to do. So there is no place to say 'this inspection requires cluster-admin read', and no way for the system to notice that the only available actor cannot.

RELATED, and deliberately not conflated: design 775f0b35 decided a WORKSPACE declares its capabilities. This is the mirror question — a STEP declaring what it requires. The two meet at the point where a system could say 'this obligation cannot be discharged by anyone currently available', which is a much better signal than a queue that silently grows.

PROPOSED, smallest first:
  1. GIVE THE SWEEP AN ACTOR THAT CAN DO IT. Either a read-only cluster-wide credential for conformance checks specifically, or route the step to David, whose admin kubeconfig can read all 31. This is a one-off and unblocks three stale packets.
  2. LET A STEP DECLARE A REQUIRED CAPABILITY, and surface an obligation nobody available can discharge rather than accumulating it. This is the durable half and needs design.

SEPARATE AND ALSO TRUE: even with a credential that reads all 31, the check verifies EXISTENCE not equality, so a green run still would not mean the cluster matches the tree (95f6aba5, already open).

MEASURED. Twelve test files in crates/core/boss-jobs/tests define a `user_header` helper. SIX serialise the real type — `serde_json::to_string(u)` where u is a `boss_policy_client::types::User` — and six BUILD THE JSON BY HAND with signatures like `user_header(id, role)` or `user_header(id, tier)`:

    terminal_report_http.rs, network_census_http.rs, stations_http.rs,
    station_projection_http.rs, stations_authoring.rs, assignments_completion.rs

THE SHAPE THEY WRITE IS ALREADY INCOMPLETE. `User` carries SIX fields — id, role, access_tier, territory_account_ids, direct_report_ids, department — and the hand-built headers write five, omitting `department`. That works today only because every optional field carries #[serde(default)].

WHY IT MATTERS. A test that hand-builds a wire shape is not testing the wire shape, it is testing a copy of it. If a field ever loses its default, or a new required one lands, these six keep passing — they construct JSON directly and never round-trip the type — while production rejects the payload. The failure would surface as a live 4xx, not as a red test, which is the wrong way round.

NOT HYPOTHETICAL AS A CLASS. Agent memory records this exact header costing ~30 minutes to rediscover: `X-Boss-User` carries JSON, not an email, and NOT the gateway's short-key session shape — a different type entirely. The shape has been got wrong before.

THE ASK: one `user_header(&User)` in boss-testing (which already owns the test-request builder in request.rs), and convert the six hand-built call sites. The good pattern already exists in the other six files; it simply is not shared. Drift then becomes a compile error rather than a silent pass.

SCOPED DELIBERATELY: this is NOT about the six identical `serde_json::to_string(u)` one-liners. Those are a fact that cannot meaningfully drift, and collapsing them alone would be churn — infra/lint/no-step-kind-match.sh's own header notes tests are exempt from some rules because they pin fixtures on purpose. The value here is making the hand-built ones serialise the real type.

metadata.detail:
FOUND BY DAVID NOTICING SOMETHING WAS MISSING. 2026-08-29: "I thought there were 2 other jobs waiting on me answering questions." There were NINE, and none of them were in his queue.

THE MECHANISM, read off the live packets. When a step completes, the step that becomes ready inherits the COMPLETER as its assignee. On backlog-item 9fa67fb9:

    filed          completed  assignee=None
    triage         completed  assignee=claude@algedonic.dev   <- I completed it
    design-review  ready      assignee=claude@algedonic.dev   <- inherited
    build          skipped    assignee=None

Every other step is unassigned. The workflow spec assigns nobody: `design-review` declares `authority_role: platform-admin` and `assignee: None`. So the assignment is entirely a runtime inheritance from the previous actor.

WHY IT IS WRONG SPECIFICALLY FOR DECISIONS. For `build` the inheritance is sensible — the person who triaged an item is a reasonable default to build it. For `design-review` it is exactly backwards: the step exists BECAUSE the triager decided they should not be the one to choose. Triaging an item to `design` is an explicit statement that a decision is needed from someone else, and the protocol then hands it back to the person who said that.

WHAT MADE IT INVISIBLE. `authority_role: platform-admin` is held by BOTH David and the agent, so nothing is violated — the step has a plausible assignee with the right authority, it just is not the right PERSON. The packets carry `owner_id: emp-david` throughout, so the correct routing target was on the record the whole time and unused. And because the steps looked assigned, they never appeared in Up-for-grabs either: they were not unclaimed, they were claimed by the wrong actor.

MEASURED CONSEQUENCE: nine design questions filed on 08-28/29 — including whether to split train.rs, how to share step-plugin code, the expedite path, the unsigned internal-service header, and the unauthenticated jobs-API back door — sat in the agent's queue where the agent cannot answer them and the owner cannot see them. David's queue showed 2; it should have shown 11.

REMEDIATED BY HAND TODAY: all nine design-review steps reassigned to their packet owner (emp-david). That is the symptom.

PROPOSED, and the choice matters:
  1. NARROW — a decision-shaped step routes to the packet OWNER rather than inheriting the completer. `owner_id` is already on every packet and `decision_shaped` is already a registry fact the assignments lens reads, so both halves exist. Smallest true fix.
  2. GENERAL — inheritance applies only when the next step shares the previous step's authority AND is not decision-shaped; otherwise the step stays unassigned and appears in Up-for-grabs, where the right person can claim it. Better long-term because it stops guessing, at the cost of more unclaimed rows.
  3. Do neither and let triage set the assignee explicitly, which is the status quo plus discipline, and therefore the one that will drift again.

RECOMMEND 1 now and 2 as the design conversation, because 1 fixes the class that actually bit and needs no new concept. RELATED: this is the mirror of the sweep finding — there, an obligation was assigned to an actor who could not discharge it (cluster-conformance, filed separately); here, an obligation was assigned to an actor who should not. Both are the same missing idea: routing follows the actor who touched it last, not the authority the work needs.

metadata.detail:
DAVID'S PROPOSAL, 2026-08-29: "Do we just track the rejected API calls? And we try to reduce that number as a sign of reliability of that step?"

Half right, and the other half would break the one thing that currently works. Both halves below.

WHY IT IS THE RIGHT INSTINCT. A refused write is the only evidence that an actor tried to complete a step according to the protocol and failed. Today the record holds successes only, which is why step conformance measures 100% (see backlog-item 2a77e5fc) — reliability is measured over survivors. A refusal is precisely a non-survivor, and it is actor-independent in exactly the sense the metric requires.

THE DATA DOES NOT EXIST. Verified, not assumed:
  - crates/core/boss-jobs/src/http/steps.rs:118-128 returns 400 from an early `return`. The OUTBOX block that emits STEP_CREATED sits BELOW it and never runs. A refused write changes nothing and therefore emits nothing.
  - `policy_rule_audit` does not cover the gap. CLAUDE.md describes it as tracking 'every policy decision', but infra/postgres/schema/04-policy.sql:63-74 constrains `kind` to rule.upsert, rule.deactivate, override.upsert, override.deactivate — it records edits to the RULEBOOK, not decisions made against it. Denials are not captured either. That doc line should be corrected regardless of what happens to this packet.

THE TRAP, AND IT IS A REAL ONE. 'Reduce that number' is Goodhart-shaped. The cheapest way to drive refusals to zero is to LOOSEN VALIDATION — and required-at-done validation is the single mechanism keeping conformance at 100%. A refusal is usually the protocol working: the 400 that stopped six proofs today (`method: expected type browser|api|log, got string`) was the step refusing bad evidence, which makes it MORE reliable, not less. A metric whose easiest win is deleting the guardrail must not be adopted as stated.

THE METRIC THAT SURVIVES THE TRAP. Do not count refusals. Count two derived things:

  1. UNRECOVERED REFUSALS — a refusal on a step never followed by a success on that same step. That is an obligation that actually went undischarged, which is the true failure. A refusal followed by a corrected write is the system working and should score as such.

  2. DISTINCT ACTORS PER (step_type, error_class) — and this is the one that makes it David's metric rather than a scoreboard. If several independent actors hit the SAME refusal on the same step, the protocol is hard to comply with: a PROTOCOL defect. If one actor hits many different refusals, that is the actor. Partitioning this way points the metric at the protocol, which is what 'regardless of which actor attempted the step' means operationally.

  Optionally 3: time-to-success after first refusal, as the friction cost of a step.

  Loosening validation cannot game this. Refusals removed by weakening a validator reappear downstream as false claims — the unmeasured half (2) of the reliability decomposition — so the incentive stays honest.

WORKED EXAMPLE, from today. `boss prove` was refused six times on `method` being prose where the field is an enum of browser|api|log. One actor, one error class, recovered in a single edit: low severity by this metric, correctly. But the underlying complaint is real and would show up the moment a second actor proves a CLI or infra change — none of those three values describes 'read the deployed artifact on the host', which is what such a proof actually does. That is the shape of a protocol defect this metric would surface on its own rather than by someone remembering to file it.

THE ONE GENUINE FORK, and it needs David. Does a refusal belong in `audit_log`? The correctness protocol holds that the log records state changes — facts about what happened — and a refusal changes nothing. But 'actor A was refused at step S for reason R' IS a fact that happened, and discarding it is exactly why the denominator is missing.
  a) A sibling table (`step_write_refusals`), keeping audit_log strictly a state-change log. Conservative; adds a second place to look.
  b) An event kind in audit_log, accepting that the log records attempts as well as outcomes. Simpler to query and rebuild from; widens what the log means.
  RECOMMEND (a) — the log's meaning is load-bearing across the five-property correctness protocol, and widening it to buy one metric is a poor trade. But it is a real fork and the answer changes what gets built.

SCOPE NOTE: this is the attempt side of the same hole that backlog-item 2a0b034e (queue-age lens) addresses from the waiting side. Together they give the metric a denominator: obligations outstanding, how long they have waited, and how often actors tried and were refused.

metadata.detail:
THE BUILD HALF of backlog-item 2a77e5fc ('Step conformance measures 100% by construction'). Specified rather than built, because the obvious implementation is the wrong one and the measurement that proves it is below.

WHAT IS NEEDED. One question the system cannot answer today: how long has this obligation been outstanding? 70 live steps sit on open IT packets right now and the only age available is the PACKET's `opened_on`, which is date-only and job-level. That is why nine design decisions could sit in the wrong actor's queue with nothing to flag them.

THE OBVIOUS FIX, AND WHY NOT. `steps.created_at` / `steps.updated_at` and `jobs.created_at` / `jobs.updated_at` already exist in Postgres (infra/postgres/schema/03-jobs.sql:27-28 and :72-73). The tempting move is to add matching fields to `boss-core::Job` and `boss-core::Step` and let them through the API. MEASURED BLAST RADIUS: `Job {` matches 63 sites and `Step {` 34 across 20+ files, concentrated in boss-jobs' integration tests plus boss-views. Rust struct literals must name every field, so `#[serde(default)]` does not save them — each site needs editing. That is a wide mechanical change to Tier-1 core, whose audit bar is the tightest in the tree, to answer one question.

RECOMMENDED INSTEAD — A LENS, NOT A FIELD. Add a read-only projection that answers the age question directly from SQL and returns its own row type, leaving `Job` and `Step` untouched:

    SELECT s.id, s.job_id, j.kind, s.spec_slug, s.status, s.assignee_id,
           s.updated_at, NOW() - s.updated_at AS waiting
      FROM steps s JOIN jobs j ON j.id = s.job_id
     WHERE s.status IN ('ready','active') AND j.status = 'open'

Zero blast radius (new port method + new row struct + one endpoint), and architecturally it is what BOSS already calls a projection — a pure function of the record. `terminal-report` is the precedent for a lens with its own shape.

WHAT `updated_at` HONESTLY GIVES. It is not a dedicated became-ready stamp: any later write bumps it. For a step sitting in `ready` that nothing has touched since it became ready — the stalled case, which is the case we care about — it IS the transition time. In general `now - updated_at` is a LOWER BOUND on the wait. That is enough to sort a queue by staleness and enough for a station to hold on age. If the bound proves too weak in practice, a dedicated `became_ready_at` is a follow-up justified by evidence rather than the opening move.

WHAT IT UNBLOCKS, beyond the metric itself:
  - a staleness lens on the queue UX, so an obligation nobody can discharge becomes visible instead of silent
  - `queue-depth` cadence rules gain an age sibling — hold on how long, not just how many
  - the actor-independent half of David's reliability metric gets a denominator: obligations outstanding and for how long, not just steps that happened to complete

NOT IN SCOPE, and it is the one thing this does not fix: user-feedback 79a5fc64 (cycle time truncating to whole days) needs a trustworthy CLOSE instant, and `jobs.updated_at` is not one — annotating a closed packet bumps it, which I did repeatedly today. The open side becomes exact via `jobs.created_at`; the close side needs either a dedicated `closed_at` or the close event's timestamp out of audit_log. Worth deciding together with this, and noted on that packet.

READY TO BUILD: the query is written, the blast radius is measured, the alternative is costed, and the honest limit of `updated_at` is stated. No open question blocks starting.

metadata.correction:
THE TIMESTAMPS ALREADY EXIST. Filed hours after the packet, on reading the schema instead of the API.

WHAT I GOT WRONG. The packet says the transition time 'is not projected' and recommends adding a `became_ready_at timestamptz` to steps as the enabling change. Both `jobs` and `steps` have carried `created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()` and `updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()` since the original table definitions — infra/postgres/schema/03-jobs.sql:27-28 (jobs) and :72-73 (steps). No migration is needed to start measuring.

WHERE THE FACT IS ACTUALLY LOST: at the DOMAIN TYPE, one layer above the database. `boss-core::Job` (crates/core/boss-core/src/job.rs:145-180) and `boss-core::Step` (:371 onward) declare neither field, so the columns are read out of Postgres into nothing and no API response can carry them. Verified against the live API: a job row returns closed_on, due_on, id, kind, metadata, opened_on, owner_id, priority, simulated, status, steps, subject, tags, title, workflow_version — and a step row returns assignee_id, blocked_by, completed_on, embedded_job, fields, id, job_id, kind, metadata, notes, sign_offs, sign_offs_required, sort_order, spec_slug, status, step_plugin_version, title. No timestamp on either, at day resolution or otherwise.

WHAT SURVIVES UNCHANGED. Every claim about consequence stands: no consumer can measure how long an obligation has waited, no station can hold on age, and the nine misrouted design decisions could not have been flagged. The three-halves decomposition stands, and so does the observation that half (1) is enforced on write and therefore always 100%.

HOW THE RECOMMENDATION CHANGES, and it changes materially. Recommendation 1 was a Tier-1 migration plus a projection change — expensive enough that I explicitly declined to build it and filed for a decision instead. The real first move is far smaller: EXPOSE THE TWO COLUMNS THAT ALREADY EXIST on Job and Step, map them in the Pg adapter, and let them through the API. Additive, no migration, no backfill, and it unblocks measurement immediately.

WHAT THE EXPOSED FIELDS DO AND DO NOT GIVE. `updated_at` is not a dedicated became-ready stamp — any later write bumps it. For a step sitting in `ready` that nothing has touched since it became ready (the common case, and exactly the stalled case we care about) it IS the transition time. In general `now - updated_at` is a LOWER BOUND on how long the step has waited, which is weaker than a dedicated column but sufficient for staleness alerting and for a queue-age lens. A dedicated `became_ready_at` becomes a follow-up justified by evidence, not the opening move.

ONE CAVEAT THE BUILD MUST HANDLE, since Job and Step are serialized into audit_log events: new fields need `#[serde(default)]` so old payloads still replay, and the rebuild UPSERT path (boss-jobs/src/rebuild.rs, which consumes jobs.step.created / jobs.step.updated as full rows) must not clobber a row's original `created_at` with the replay's own NOW().

SAME ROOT CAUSE, SEPARATE PACKET: user-feedback 79a5fc64 ('Cycle time truncates to whole days, so a 30-minute pipeline measures 0') is this identical gap at job level. Its report blames `num_days()` truncating in boss-jobs/src/port.rs:262, but `opened_on` and `closed_on` are DATE columns, so the precision was never there to truncate — while `jobs.created_at` next to them holds the real instant and is dropped at the same domain-type boundary. That packet cannot be fixed without this one, and gets most of the way there with it: the open side becomes exact, and only a trustworthy CLOSE instant is still missing (`updated_at` is unreliable for that, since annotating a closed packet bumps it — something I did repeatedly today).

The general lesson is the one this packet already names, now with a third instance and a sharper edge: read the schema, not the API response, before concluding a fact is not recorded. The API is a projection and projections drop things silently.

PROMPTED BY DAVID'S DEFINITION, 2026-08-29: "How reliably was a step completed according to the protocol, regardless of which actor attempted to complete the step." This packet is the attempt to MEASURE that, and what the attempt found.

MEASUREMENT 1 — field conformance, and why the number is worthless.
Every workflow step declares `fields` with `required: true`. A completed step either carries them or it does not. Measured across every open and closed job in the nine IT protocols, comparing each step to the workflow version ITS OWN PACKET was admitted under:

    3,517 completed steps measured, 0 short -> 100.0% conformant

Every step of every protocol: 100%. ship-a-change scope/build/gate/review/proven, pr-train all eight steps, user-feedback triage/investigate, maintenance-sweep inspect/remediate, protocol-retro all four, approval decide.

The number is 100% because it CANNOT be anything else. Required-at-done validators run on the write path, so a step physically cannot reach `completed` without its required fields. The measurement certifies the validator, not the work. It carries zero information about reliability.

(A first pass got this wrong in an instructive way. Comparing every completed step to the CURRENT spec instead of the packet's pinned version reported ship-a-change `proven` at 23.1% and would have started a fire. `proof` became required at v22; a v18 packet completing `proven` without it was fully conformant to the protocol it was admitted under. The 83 'violations' were the protocol getting STRICTER over time, which is version pinning working exactly as designed. Any future conformance report has to resolve the pinned version or it will keep manufacturing this same false alarm.)

MEASUREMENT 2 — what is outstanding, and the fact the record does not hold.
70 live steps sit on open IT packets: 34 backlog-item, 20 user-feedback, 11 ship-a-change, 5 maintenance-sweep. 59 wait on the agent, 11 on David. Age distribution by PACKET age: 38 at 0-1d, 15 at 2-6d, 17 at 7-29d, none over 30d.

That age is a proxy, and a weak one, because THE RECORD CANNOT SAY WHEN A STEP BECAME READY. A step row carries exactly one timestamp — `completed_on` — and it is date-only. There is no `ready_on`, no `started_at`, no `updated_at`. So for any outstanding obligation the system cannot answer 'how long has this been waiting', only 'how old is the packet that contains it'.

THE STRUCTURAL POINT. David's metric asks how reliably a step was completed. The record can only answer that for steps that DID complete — and for those, the answer is definitionally 100%. Steps that were supposed to complete and did not contribute nothing to the denominator, because there is no denominator. Reliability today is measured over survivors.

WHERE THE ACTUAL FAILURES LIVE. Every failure this week was invisible to measurement 1 and unmeasurable by measurement 2:
  - a gate-run closed `lost` while a green verdict existed -> `record-verdict` 100% conformant, VALUE wrong
  - `proven` recorded on a change that shipped `on_missing='warn'` while claiming `abort` -> conformant, CLAIM false
  - 'Settled - carry it to a file' completed with no file written -> conformant, EFFECT absent
  - nine design decisions sat ready in the wrong actor's queue -> never completed, so never counted
  - 8 of 9 spawned class-fix cars abandoned, 7 with no reason -> `abandon_reason` is not required, so not measured
  - a cluster-conformance sweep verified 2 of 31 objects -> `inspect` conformant, coverage unknown

So the metric decomposes into three halves and BOSS enforces only the first:
  1. Does the completed step carry what the protocol requires? ENFORCED on write. Always 100%.
  2. Is what it carries TRUE? Unmeasured.
  3. Did the obligation get discharged at all, and how long did it wait? UNMEASURABLE — no transition timestamp.

GOOD NEWS ON (3): the fact is not lost, only unprojected. `jobs.step.updated` publishes the FULL step row on every transition and lands in audit_log; boss-jobs/src/rebuild.rs consumes exactly that to reconstruct step state. The log is the system of record and it holds every transition with a real timestamp. The projection simply drops it, and no door exposes it — /api/events/tail is served by boss-events, not by the jobs API that boss-api is pinned to, so the tooling every session actually uses cannot reach it.

RECOMMENDED, smallest true fix first:
  1. PROJECT THE TRANSITION TIME. A nullable `became_ready_at timestamptz` on steps, set where the registry flips a step to ready. Additive, no backfill needed (it starts measuring from the day it lands), and it turns 'how long has this obligation been outstanding' into a query. This is the enabling change — (3) is unmeasurable without it and stations cannot hold on age without it either.
  2. GENERALIZE THE PROBE. `boss prove --probe --expect --verified` is the ONE place BOSS made a step's claim checkable by machine rather than assertable by an actor, and it exists on exactly one step of one workflow. The pattern generalizes: a terminal declares a probe that verifies its own claim. That is the only mechanism on the table that attacks half (2), and half (2) is where the expensive failures are.
  3. REQUIRE THE REASON ON TERMINALS THAT DESTROY WORK. `abandon_reason` on ship-a-change's `abandoned` was already proposed and is still awaiting go-ahead; the 7-of-9 reasonless abandons are exactly the case.

WHAT I DID NOT DO. I did not build (1) — it is a Tier-1 core migration plus a projection change, and it is the substrate half of a metric David is still defining. Filing with the numbers first. If the answer is 'just build it', it is well-scoped and additive.

RELATED: this is the third finding this week with the same shape — the record contains a fact that no projection surfaces and no door reaches, so an operator concludes the fact does not exist. The other two were the cadence split-brain (`last-firing` returns null because cadence_firings is empty on the cluster) and the nine misrouted decisions (`owner_id` was on every packet, unused).

MEASURED 2026-08-29 while draining the sweep queue.

THE MECHANISM. infra/dispatcher/rules.toml:646-652 and :672-678 both read:

    schedule = { cadence = "daily", anchor_date = "2026-08-17" }
    [[rule.do]]
    handler = "jobs.spawn"

There is no condition. The rule fires daily and spawns a packet whether or not the previous day's packet was ever touched. Nothing consults the state of the obligation it is about to duplicate.

WHAT THAT HAS PRODUCED. 5 open maintenance-sweep packets, all from two rules:
  cluster-conformance: 3 open — f45d97cc (08-27), cace2f50 (08-28), 3e24e2cb (08-29)
  doc-status:          2 open — 6268ae28 (08-28), 6e124efc (08-29)
Of those, cace2f50 has never even been INSPECTED: its inspect step is still `ready` a day later, so the 08-28 obligation was replaced by an identical 08-29 one before anyone looked at it.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN UNTIDY, for cluster-conformance specifically. That sweep's own 08-29 inspection concluded it CANNOT be discharged by the actor it is given to: 31 objects declared across infra/cluster/manifests/, 2 verified present, 0 missing, and 29 unreadable with the dev-session credential. I confirmed the credential shape independently today — /etc/boss-dev/kubeconfig authenticates as system:serviceaccount:boss-dev:dev-session, which cannot read namespaces or nodes and is scoped to boss-dev, while the manifests span other namespaces. So this is not a backlog that will drain when someone finds time. It is a rule minting one undischargeable obligation per day, indefinitely, and the queue depth is the only thing that will ever change.

HOW IT STAYED INVISIBLE. Each packet individually looks fine — recent, well-formed, with a real inspection on the newest one. It is only visible by counting packets per target, which no surface does. It is also invisible to the step-conformance measure (backlog-item 2a77e5fc): every step these packets DID complete carries every required field, so they score 100% while the obligation goes undischarged. This is the denominator problem in its purest form — the packets that measure worst are the ones that contribute nothing to the measurement.

OPTIONS, and they are not exclusive:
  1. SPAWN CONDITIONALLY — skip if an open packet already exists for the same (kind, subject/target). Smallest, and it converts a growing queue into a single standing obligation that stays visible. Risk: a sweep that is stuck stops producing new evidence, so the ONE packet must then be loud rather than quiet, which argues for pairing this with the queue-age lens in backlog-item 2a0b034e.
  2. SUPERSEDE ON SPAWN — spawn the new one and close the predecessor with an explicit `superseded` outcome naming its replacement. Keeps a daily datapoint and keeps the queue at one. More faithful to what a daily check is for, and it leaves the trail that option 1 discards.
  3. FIX THE CAPABILITY for cluster-conformance — a read-only credential that can actually see the 29 objects. This is a credential change and therefore David's, and it is orthogonal: without 1 or 2 the accumulation continues for any sweep that stalls for any reason.

RECOMMEND 2 + 3. Option 2 because a maintenance sweep exists to produce a daily datapoint, and option 1 silently stops producing them precisely when something is wrong — the failure mode this system keeps rediscovering, where a check that cannot run looks the same as a check that passed. Option 3 because until the actor can read what it is asked to verify, the sweep's honest verdict is 'unknown', and it says so today rather than claiming clean, which is the one part of this that is working exactly as designed.

NOT DONE HERE, deliberately: I did not complete `remediate` on any of the five to clear the queue. Four of them have real, unfinished work behind them, and completing a step whose work is not done is precisely the failure the reliability metric is meant to catch. The doc-status pair is separately blocked — its 146 stranded decisions would be flushed into markdown files that the approved packet-migration then deletes, and the documented `boss docs flush-pending` points at boss-gcp's SEPARATE index (52 docs, 0 queued), so it would report success having flushed nothing.

metadata.detail:
THE SYMPTOM. The stat board's 'median cycle' renders '0d' for everything. It is not a display bug: port.rs:263 computes `(closed_on - job.opened_on).num_days() as f64` and BOTH are NaiveDate, so the measurement has one-day resolution by construction. An IT department that ships in hours cannot be measured by a number that can only be 0 or 1.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS WRONG. `Job` (boss-core/src/job.rs:145) carries opened_on/due_on/closed_on as DATES and no timestamps at all, so the pure report function structurally cannot see an instant. Adding a timestamp field to `Job` means editing 62 struct-literal construction sites across boss-core, boss-jobs, boss-views, boss-sim and boss-dispatcher-handlers - there is no Default to lean on. That is a churny cross-crate change for one number.

WHAT THE DATA ALREADY HAS. The `jobs` table carries `created_at TIMESTAMPTZ` (real open instant). `updated_at` is NOT usable as a close instant: annotating a closed packet via PATCH /api/jobs/{id}/metadata moves it, and this session does that routinely. Steps DO carry real instants - the conductor stamps `completed_at` on 31/31 review steps today, and car edeb691b adds park's and prove's - but the report is a function of &[Job] and Job has no steps.

THE CONSTRAINT THAT DECIDES THE DESIGN. Postgres OVERRIDES the report with one SQL statement (postgres.rs:1101) and tests/terminal_report_pg.rs pins that SQL to the pure function 'formula-for-formula'. So any fix must land in BOTH and keep them reading the SAME source, or it breaks a stated and tested invariant.

RECOMMENDED DESIGN - stamp the instants into JOB METADATA, which both paths can already read:
  1. At job create, write metadata.opened_at (RFC3339). At close, write metadata.closed_at using the SAME instant the close already uses for closed_on. There are exactly TWO close hooks, both in http/steps.rs and both already holding a `now`: line 867 (auto-close on a terminal step, `step.completed_on.or(job_now)`) and line 1392.
  2. Pure fn: cycle = closed_at - opened_at when both are present, else fall back to (closed_on - opened_on) * 24. Report HOURS, not days.
  3. SQL: the same expression over metadata->>'opened_at' / metadata->>'closed_at' with the same fallback. Parity holds because both read one source.
  4. Web: yard.ts `days()` (line 748) formats sub-day - minutes under an hour, hours under a day.

WHY METADATA RATHER THAN A COLUMN: no migration, no Job-struct change, no 62-site edit, and it is how BOSS already records instants - ship-a-change v28 puts `completed_at` in STEP metadata for exactly this reason. Going-forward only, which is what David asked for: 'put the proper fields into the protocol to fill out going forward'. Do NOT backfill audit_log - decided against on 2026-08-28.

SEPARATING QUEUE FROM WORK IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN THIS ITEM. It needs the step stamps to be flowing in production, and car edeb691b (which makes park and prove write them) is parked, not merged. Building the split now would ship a feature with no data behind it and nothing to prove it with. The natural home is the yard board, which already fetches cars WITH their steps: dock queue is gate.completed_at -> review.completed_at, train+proof is review.completed_at -> proven.completed_at. Sequence it after edeb691b lands and new cars have parked.

NOT MEASURABLE EITHER WAY: coding time. The car packet does not exist until `boss park` creates it, so everything before park is outside the packet's life. If we want real work time the honest source is the branch's first commit, read at park time, as a new field.

MEASURED 2026-08-29, cost one wasted 11-minute gate and one falsely-lost packet.

WHAT HAPPENS. `boss gate <branch>` creates a runner Job and exits, printing:

    boss gate: not waiting — `boss gate --wait` follows it, or read the packet.

Following that advice literally is the bug. The second invocation does NOT attach to the running Job: it REUSES the open gate-run packet ('boss gate: reusing open gate-run packet 26ac72a0') and creates a SECOND runner Job against it. Two Jobs then race on the same gate-target PVC. On 2026-08-29 gate-vtkc4 died 70s in with the pod in Error; gate-2cn2l survived, ran the full gate, and went GREEN.

THE COMPOUND FAILURE. While gate-2cn2l was still running, the `--wait` guard from car de2f89ab noticed a dead Job and did exactly what it was built to do — it stopped instead of hanging — and closed the packet: verdict `lost`, receipt 'runner died before a receipt: line 82'. So the guard is correct in isolation and wrong here, because it does not ask whether ANOTHER Job for the same packet is still alive. The gate that actually ran was green and the record says lost.

TWO CANDIDATE FIXES, both small:
  1. `boss gate` on a branch that already has a live Job for its open packet should ATTACH (poll it) rather than create a second one — which is what the closing line already promises. If attaching is not wanted, refuse and name the running Job.
  2. The `--wait` dead-Job guard should scope its 'nothing is coming' conclusion to the Job it is actually following, or check for a live sibling before declaring `lost`.

WHY IT IS WORTH A PACKET. The CLI's own guidance produced the failure, so 'read the help more carefully' is not the fix. This is the class the doors list in CLAUDE.md exists to close: a door that stops being true is a defect worth a car.

MEASURED 2026-08-29: `--recheck` run against 10 recently-proven cars. 7 HOLDS, 3 NO LONGER HOLDS. All three failures are PROBE DEFECTS, not regressions — the underlying behaviour was re-verified by hand and still holds in every case. That is a 30% false-alarm rate on the one instrument built to detect decay.

THE THREE, and the single root cause:

  932aa956 and 3f846cc5 — recorded probe begins `ssh boss-gcp "..."`. The probe was AUTHORED on the workstation, where `boss-gcp` is a name in ~/.ssh/config, and is RE-RUN on boss-gcp, where it resolves to nothing:
      stderr: ssh: Could not resolve hostname boss-gcp: Temporary failure in name resolution
    3f846cc5's claim was re-verified directly on boss-gcp and DOES hold — `boss gate --mode bogus` still prints '`--mode bogus` is not a gate mode'. This is the probe shape the 2026-08-28 note singled out as the DURABLE one, so the durable shape is being defeated by a portability bug rather than by decay.

  64d5e3c7 — probe opens with `git rev-parse --short HEAD` and assumes a repository as cwd:
      stderr: fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git

SO THE VERB RECORDS AN INCOMPLETE ARTIFACT. `boss prove` captures the command, exit status and both streams — but not the two pieces of context the command needs to mean the same thing twice: WHICH HOST it ran on and WHICH DIRECTORY. Without them `--recheck` is not re-running the proof, it is running a different one.

PROPOSED, smallest first:
  1. Record `host` and `cwd` alongside the probe at prove time (both are free — the verb already knows them).
  2. `--recheck` re-establishes cwd, and REFUSES with a clear message when it is invoked on a different host than the proof was recorded on, instead of reporting NO LONGER HOLDS. A probe that cannot be re-run is not the same fact as a claim that stopped being true, and today they are rendered identically.
  3. Optionally lint at prove time: a probe naming `ssh <host>` where <host> is the host running the probe is almost always the workstation-authoring mistake.

WHY THE DISTINCTION IS LOAD-BEARING. The whole point of `proven` requiring a machine-run probe is that a machine, not a sentence, saw the thing. An instrument that cries wolf 30% of the time gets ignored, and then decay stops being detected at all.

COUNTED 2026-08-29: 6 lookups in one drain needed a list-then-filter pass purely to turn a short id into a full one.

THE ASYMMETRY. Every packet in this system is REFERRED TO by its 8-char prefix — journals, arrival reports, skip reasons, this retro, David's own messages. `boss prove <car>` accepts 'its branch, or 8+ characters of its id' and resolves it. But `GET /api/jobs/44f121e4` answers:

    invalid job id  (HTTP 400)

so any tooling holding the id everything else prints has to fetch a LIST, filter client-side, and only then fetch the packet. That is 2 round trips and a scan for a lookup, and it is why `getid.py`-shaped scratch scripts keep getting rewritten per session — the same class the retro warns about, since a fresh shell pipeline answers confidently either way.

MAKES IT WORSE: list endpoints filter by `kind`, so the list-and-filter pass ALSO has to already know the workflow kind. Looking up a bare prefix with an unknown kind means iterating kinds. That combination is what turned a one-line lookup into a 40-line script three times tonight.

PREFER FIXING WHAT EXISTS. The resolver is already written — it lives in boss-cli behind `boss prove`. The gap is that it is one verb's private convenience rather than a property of the id. Two candidate shapes, cheapest first:
  1. Accept an unambiguous prefix on `GET /api/jobs/{id}`, 404 on no match and 409 on ambiguity. Prefix resolution already has to answer 'ambiguous' somewhere, so this is where it belongs.
  2. Failing that, lift the resolver out of `boss prove` into something every verb and the `boss-api` door can call, so at least there is ONE implementation instead of a scratch script per session.

NOT PROPOSED: making callers use full uuids. The system prints prefixes everywhere by design (see the standing rule to refer to packets by protocol + title rather than bare uuids); the ids humans and agents actually hold are the short ones.

MEASURED 2026-08-29 across all 12 bundles in infra/step-plugins (4,454 lines).

  9 of 12 define their own `h()` DOM helper — in FOUR distinct implementations
  3 of 12 define their own `esc()`
  2 of 12 implement their own markdown rendering

  3. ACCEPT IT and pin the divergence with a test asserting all copies behave identically (CLAUDE.md 9a's holding action).

That difference was previously mis-attributed to the packets being low-stakes; they are not low-stakes, they are contextless.

CLASS A - an ad-hoc check produced a confident WRONG answer (7 of 14, exactly half):
  1. `grep -c ... || echo 0` printed "0\n0", which compared unequal to "0", so a wait loop reported a file had changed when it had not. FAILED OPEN.
  2. `git merge-base --is-ancestor gcp/<branch> <main>` reported NOT MERGED for all 89 cars, because arrived trains delete their branches and a missing ref makes merge-base error. FAILED CLOSED.
  3. Testing the car's receipt sha reported NOT MERGED for all 89, because trains squash-merge so a car's commit is never an ancestor. FAILED CLOSED.
  4. Content-checking against `gcp/realmain` reported the change absent; that ref is a stale local alias and not what trains merge into. FAILED CLOSED.
  5. `rc=$?` after a pipeline measured `tail`, not the command under test. FAILED OPEN.
  6. `kubectl get jobs | grep -v Complete | tail -2` hid the running gate and showed two 20h-old failures, producing a false 'nothing is running'. FAILED CLOSED.

CLASS B - a value typed instead of read (2): a hand-authored UUID (the sixth-plus occurrence), and zsh applying `:r` as a parameter modifier to `$B:refs/heads/$B`, mangling a refspec into `refs/tmp/<branch>efs/heads/<branch>` while the following `&&` chain deleted the temp ref and reported success.

CLASS C - acted on state that was never declared (2): a kubectl RBAC grant that was drift and silently reverted on converge, blocking all gating; and `POST /api/workflows/{kind}/publish`, which takes no body and promoted a stale v16 draft, regressing ship-a-change from v19 to v16 in production.

CLASS D - asserted about another environment without checking (2): told David to `git fetch` a branch that exists only on the forge, which his GitHub-backed clone cannot see; and concluded 'no admin access exists' from two absences when the admin kubeconfig was present at /Users/david/talos-homelab/v2/kubeconfig.

CLASS E - a test whose assertion was wrong (1): asserted a refspec must not contain "efs/heads", which is a substring of the correct "refs/heads".

THE DISTRIBUTION IS THE FINDING. Half of all errors are Class A, and every Class A and Class B failure happened IN THE SHELL. Not one occurred inside a tested Rust verb. The shell is where a fresh, untested verification pipeline gets written per question, and it answers confidently either way - five of the seven Class A failures answered 'no' for reasons unrelated to the question asked.

THE MECHANISM THAT ALREADY WORKS: promote a repeated hand-check into a verb with tests. Three shipped in one day and each retired a failure class AND caught a real error on its first use:
  - `boss park` retired receipt transcription -> refused a car whose branch had moved past its receipt (932aa956's own fix, catching the author).
  - `boss prove` retired evidence-by-assertion -> refused `boss park --help` on a stale binary, and its unit test reproduces the grep-c bug above so that specific lie cannot return.
  - `boss publish` retired the two-hop shell dance -> verified both of its own pushes against the forge, and its test caught a wrong assertion in ITSELF before shipping.

WHAT IS MISSING, in priority order:
1. CLASS A HAS NO VERB. The questions asked repeatedly in shell are still hand-rolled every time: 'is this branch actually merged?', 'which release is deployed and does it carry this change?', 'what does this car's receipt vouch for?'. Each was written fresh today and each was wrong. These are three functions with tests, not three pipelines per session. Highest value by a wide margin - 50% of errors.
2. NOTHING MEASURES RELIABILITY. A lying check is only noticed when it bites; there is no metric, so 'are we getting better?' is currently answered by impression. Cheap first version: count, per session, how many verification questions were answered by a verb versus a fresh shell pipeline. That ratio is the reliability number, and it is the same argument the terminal-report makes for delivery.
3. NOTHING RE-RUNS PROOFS (filed 2b30eff4). Class C is proof decay, and a scheduled `boss prove --recheck` sweep would have caught the RBAC revert within a day rather than when the next gate happened to run.

THE GENERALISATION WORTH KEEPING: reliability here is not carefulness, it is SURFACE. Every verb built removes a category of question from the shell, and the shell is where the errors live. So the codebase-should-shrink instinct and the reliability goal point the same way - each verb should retire the hand-work it replaces, and the measure of the pipeline is how many questions can be answered without writing a new pipeline to answer them.

The verb erred out and returned non-zero, which to a caller looks exactly like a failed gate. A poll loop against a service that restarts on every deploy should retry a connection error for a bounded window and only give up if it persists; the packet is the record, and the packet was fine.

This is the class car 28662b18 exists for one level up - 'a dropped lookup does not red a train' - and the same reasoning applies to the gate verb: a momentary absence is not evidence of failure. Worse, an agent that reads 'Connection refused' as a red gate will re-gate, spending another ~11 minutes of cluster time for a run that was already healthy. The load-bearing refusal: if a draft already exists that is NOT the one being published, refuse and say what is sitting there, because that is exactly the state that promoted v16.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND CONVENIENCE: protocol is meant to be cheap to iterate - that is the whole argument for workflows being registry data. Observed 2026-08-28 on packet c0b7e73d:

    packet metadata sha : b64ed98856e261e9a7373b69ccbd53d3ddc9af32
    receipt head        : 3647092b2279453606b60b08d8182b999f34bd7e
    runner log          : feat/parking-a-car-is-a-verb@3647092b22 -> green

Two different commits, one packet. `boss gate` resolves a sha with `git ls-remote origin <branch>` on the machine it runs on and writes THAT into the packet; the gate-runner then clones from the FORGE, checks the branch out, and derives the head from what it actually got. When those two sources disagree, the packet records a commit that was never gated.

THE GOOD NEWS FIRST, because it bounds the damage. The receipt is truthful — it reports what the runner checked out, not what the packet claimed — and the receipt is what `boss park` copies onto a car. So no car has ever carried a head that was not gated. The integrity that matters holds.

WHAT BREAKS ANYWAY: `reusable_packet` matches an open packet on branch AND sha, using the packet's stale field. So after a rebase, a fresh `boss gate` sees no match, files a SECOND packet for the same branch, and the first is orphaned — precisely the orphan the verb was written to prevent. It also means the packet's own metadata cannot be trusted to answer 'what was gated', which is the first question anyone asks of it.

HOW THE DISAGREEMENT ARISES. `origin` is hardcoded. On boss-gcp origin IS the forge and the two agree. Anywhere else it does not: from a workstation `origin` is GitHub, the branch is usually absent, and resolution falls back to a symbolic ref — or, with a GIT_CONFIG insteadOf override pointed at the conductor's clone (the workaround used all night), it resolves against THAT clone's local branches, which are only as fresh as the last push to them. That is how a rebased branch produced a sha two commits behind.

ROUTES.
(1) Resolve against the forge explicitly rather than `origin` — read BOSS_TRAIN_FORGE_URL/REPO the way train.rs already does, so the sha comes from the same place the runner will clone from. This also retires the insteadOf workaround and the symbolic-ref fallback, and is the same route already proposed on the RBAC item.
(2) Failing that, have the runner WRITE BACK the head it actually checked out into the packet metadata, so the packet stops disagreeing with its own receipt.
(3) Make `reusable_packet` match on branch alone among OPEN packets, and let the sha be advisory — an open gate-run for a branch is the thing worth reusing regardless of which commit it was filed against, since a rebase does not make the packet less orphaned.

(1) is the fix; (3) is worth doing regardless because it is what makes reuse survive a rebase.

Damage stays bounded because the RECEIPT is truthful and it is the receipt `boss park` copies, so no car has carried an ungated head; the defect is that the packet lies and reuse keys on the lie. CONTEXT: `boss prove` (shipped 2026-08-28, car 25da5be3) records a re-runnable probe on the `proven` step and `--recheck` re-runs it. Decay is therefore DETECTABLE. It is not DETECTED - nothing runs the rechecks, so a proof that stopped holding stays a green sentence in a closed packet until someone happens to look.

IT ALREADY HAPPENED, same day. Car 932aa956's probe observed a real production refusal, then stopped holding within the hour because the condition it keyed on was transient. `--recheck` reports NO LONGER HOLDS correctly and is wrong about the cause. Contrast 3f846cc5 and 25da5be3, whose probes are durable and still hold.

TWO ASKS, both small:
1. A cadence job that runs `boss prove <car> --recheck` across recently-closed cars and files a packet naming any that stopped holding. That turns proof from a one-shot stamp into a standing assertion, which is the only version that catches a silent revert - the exact failure infra/push-step-plugins.sh warns about, where a ConfigMap preview survives until the next converge.
2. A way to REPLACE a decayed proof. `boss prove` refuses a step that is already completed, so today the only route from a transient proof to a durable one is an operator edit of job metadata. Re-proving with a better probe should be a first-class move, and the old proof should be kept rather than overwritten - a proof that used to hold and no longer does is evidence about the system, not a mistake to erase.

NOT ASKED FOR: judging whether a probe is a good probe. That stays human; the recorded proof shows what was asserted so a reader can challenge it.

infra/gate-runner/gate-runner.yaml declares `imagePullSecrets: [{name: forgejo-registry}]`, but that Secret exists only in namespace `boss`:

  boss       forgejo-registry   kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson   17d
  boss-dev   (absent)

Gate Jobs run in `boss-dev`. A named-but-absent imagePullSecret is not an error to Kubernetes - it is silently ignored - so pulls fall back to anonymous, and today they succeed only because the images are already in each node's cache.

WHY IT MATTERS LATER, NOT NOW. Nothing is broken and nothing will be, until a gate is scheduled onto a node with a cold cache - a new worker node, an evicted image, or a tag that has moved. Then the gate fails at pull with ImagePullBackOff, which reads as an infrastructure outage rather than a missing Secret, and it happens on whichever node happens to be new. w-1 and w-2 are 2 days old; the next node added is the likely trigger.

Noticed while enumerating consumers for the forge-token rotation (rotate-a-credential packet, Subject `forge-token`), so it is worth deciding TOGETHER with that: if the registry Secret is minted from the same forge token, it has to be rotated too, and this is the moment its absence in boss-dev gets fixed.

boss-dev.yaml line 30 already carries the recipe as a comment - copy the Secret from `boss` into the target namespace. Either do that for boss-dev, or drop the imagePullSecret from gate-runner.yaml and say plainly that gate images are pulled anonymously. What should not stand is a manifest that claims a credential it does not have.

FIXED: the Secret was copied into boss-dev (value moved namespace-to-namespace without passing through a terminal). Verified present: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson, 1 key.

The design recorded on 398914e0 is to mirror the kaniko executor and the bun base image into the forge registry and pin them by digest. That makes this Secret load-bearing rather than decorative: once gate images come from 10.20.0.15:3000, a missing pull secret stops every gate rather than being masked by cache. Fixing it first is what makes that change safe.

Nine access tokens exist for forge user `david`. One is attributed. The audit run on 2026-08-27 says:

  9 declared, 9 live for user 'david'
    UNATTRIBUTED  8 declared token(s) still have consumer = UNKNOWN
    BREADTH       3 tokens carry write:repository
                  (boss-gcp, dev-pod-push-20260821, push-20260818)
  EXIT=2

WHY THIS IS THE ITEM AND NOT JUST UNTIDINESS. A credential nobody can attribute is a credential nobody dares revoke: revoking it might break something, and nobody can say what. So it is kept, forever, and the count only goes up. That is exactly what blocked revocation on 2026-08-27 - identifying the disclosed token needed a read-only query against the forge's SQLite database, because the UI shows only name and scope and the names encode dates (`push-20260818`) rather than holders.

THE MECHANISM IS ALREADY BUILT. infra/platform/forge-tokens.toml declares the inventory and `maintenance-forge-token-audit` reports drift weekly. It refuses to report clean while any consumer is UNKNOWN, so this item has an automatic, unambiguous done condition: the audit exits 0. The audit deliberately cannot fix this itself - deleting a credential is administration and stays with a human.

STARTING POINTS, cheapest first.

1. `cluster-registry` (write:package) - created 2026-08-10 21:13 UTC and last used the same minute, superseded by `cluster-registry2` sixty seconds later. Almost certainly a mis-mint that was immediately redone. Safest first deletion in the set.

2. `push-20260818` (write:repository) - its last-used jumped to 2026-08-27 23:17 UTC, the exact minute of the post-rotation dev-pod check, and has not moved since. That is evidence it was the value in Secret boss-dev/forge-read until that Secret was overwritten. If confirmed it is now UNHELD, and it carries write:repository for consumers that only clone. Confirming it retires an UNKNOWN and identifies a deletion candidate at once. Tracked separately by the rotate-a-credential packet on Subject `forge-read`.

3. `k8s-pull` (read:package) and `image-push-20260812` (write:package) - last used the same minute, 2026-08-27 21:45 UTC, which suggests both are exercised by the image pull/push path. One of them is probably behind Secret boss/forgejo-registry. Checking that Secret's value against each identifies it.

4. `boss-dev-read`, `boss-ci-package`, `cluster-registry2`, `dev-pod-push-20260821` - names suggest holders; none confirmed.

METHOD THAT AVOIDS GUESSING: for a candidate token, compute the SHA-256 of the value held by the suspected consumer (a Secret, a file) and compare digests. That attributes a token without either value being printed anywhere - it is how the conductor's file and boss-dev/forge-read were confirmed identical during the rotation.

AND WHEN NAMING THE NEXT ONE: name tokens after the consumer that holds them, not the date they were minted. `boss-gcp` is answerable a month later; `push-20260818` is not.

metadata.body:
SECURITY SCANNING ONLY HAPPENS AT PUBLISH TIME, so a fortnight of code accumulates unscanned
and arrives as one wall of alerts on a PR that is already asking for a decision.

WHAT HAPPENED. Publish PR algedonic-dev/boss#236 (94 commits, 874 files) went red on CodeQL
with 46 alerts - 19 critical, 27 high. None of it had been seen before, because CodeQL runs in
.github/workflows/ci.yml on the PUBLIC MIRROR only. The internal forge CI (.forgejo/workflows/
ci.yml) has build-image, locomotive, web, fast and test - no static security analysis at all.
So every car since 2026-08-12 was gated, boarded, merged, deployed and PROVEN without any of
its code being security-scanned.

TRIAGED, so the number is not the story:
  46 alerts -> 34 in test code, 12 in production code.
  The 34 are fixtures: local_auth.rs's "hard-coded cryptographic value" hits are all inside
  #[cfg(test)] (starts line 811) on literals like "pw" and "correct horse battery", and the
  rest are integration tests under tests/ which carry no #[cfg(test)] marker.
  The 12 production findings collapse to one pattern plus outliers:
    - 8x service-to-service identity over plain HTTP. passkey.rs:270 and tenant_data.rs
      (5 sites) send x-boss-user {"id":"automation:gateway","role":"platform-admin"} to
      internal URLs over http, and because the URL is built with format!, CodeQL also calls
      it SSRF. Real architectural observation - internal traffic is unencrypted and identity
      is asserted by header - not an internet-facing hole.
    - reindex.rs:49 and shape_driven/tenant.rs:827, uncontrolled data in a path expression.
    - sign-off.js:61, "DOM text reinterpreted as HTML", on a line that is
      document.createTextNode(String(child)) - the safe path. Reads as a false positive.

AND IT IS NOT ALL PRE-EXISTING. CodeQL warns that a large diff surfaces alerts it did not
introduce, which is true of http_client.rs and tenant_data.rs. But passkey.rs and
sign-off.js are NEW in this PR - the passkey ceremony and the sign-off plugin were both
written since 2026-08-12. So the header-over-HTTP pattern is newly authored code that no gate
questioned, not merely old code newly scanned.

WHY THIS IS A PROTOCOL GAP AND NOT A BACKLOG OF BUGS. The findings are individually modest.
The problem is WHEN they arrive: at the moment of publishing, against a 94-commit diff, with
no way to attribute a finding to the car that wrote it. A gate that runs per-car would have
put the passkey header pattern in front of the person writing the passkey ceremony, while
they still had it in their head. Instead it lands on the owner as a publish blocker weeks
later, which is the most expensive possible place to learn it.

WHAT TO DO. Add static security analysis to the forge gate so it runs per car, not per
publish. Full CodeQL needs GitHub, but the forge can run `cargo audit` for advisories and
`cargo clippy` already carries some of this; the closer equivalent is running CodeQL's CLI in
the boss-ci image, or accepting a narrower scanner and being explicit about the gap that
leaves. Whatever is chosen, the invariant to hold is: no car is proven in prod on code that
nothing has security-scanned.

RELATED: my own publish review declared the diff publishable on the strength of
infra/lint/no-secrets.sh being clean. That lint looks for credential MATERIAL and found none,
correctly - and CodeQL then found twelve production issues it was never designed to see.
Treating a clean secrets scan as clearance for a public push is too narrow a test, and the
publish protocol's review step should say which question each check actually answers.

metadata.body:
THE JOBS API BACK DOOR IS UNAUTHENTICATED AND REACHABLE FROM THE HOUSE LAN. A client on
the home network can assume platform-admin with no credential.

This is the gap between the documented trust model and the running deployment — not a
surprise in the code, a mis-deploy around a limitation SECURITY.md names explicitly.

THE MODEL (SECURITY.md 'Deployment trust model'). BOSS authenticates at ONE boundary,
boss-gateway. The gateway strips inbound x-boss-* headers at its edge and injects identity
from the signed session cookie; backends then trust x-boss-user VERBATIM. The whole model
rests on one sentence: 'the gateway must be the only thing that can reach the backend
service ports.'

THE VIOLATION. boss-jobs-internal is a LoadBalancer on 10.20.0.34:7900 with NodePort 31047
on EVERY node. That is the opposite of 'only the gateway can reach it'. Verified from a
Mac on the house LAN (192.168.1.110), which is NOT on the cluster VLAN:

    GET 10.20.0.34:7900/api/jobs, no identity header        -> 200 (real data)
    GET 10.20.0.34:7900/api/jobs, forged x-boss-user admin  -> 200 (real data)
    GET 10.20.0.11:31047 / .14:31047 / .16:31047 (NodePort) -> 200 each

The machine-token gate that would stop writes (BOSS_MACHINE_TOKEN, feedback 7fcd78fa
phase 1) is DORMANT everywhere. The running jobs API logged it itself at 23:21 on
2026-08-26: 'no BOSS_MACHINE_TOKEN configured: the machine door accepts unauthenticated
writes'. machine_gate.rs confirms: with no token the gate admits everything. A forged
WRITE was NOT executed — the classifier blocked it, correctly — but reads, the dormant
gate, and the code path together are conclusive.

WHAT IS SAFE, established by probing rather than assumed:
- THE FRONT DOOR. playground.algedonic.dev is double-gated: Cloudflare Access (every
  request in the Caddy logs carries Cf-Access-Authenticated-User-Email + a
  Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion, so only allowlisted identities reach the tunnel) AND the
  gateway's own login (argon2, signed session, SameSite=Strict, edge-strip). You cannot
  forge identity through it.
- THE PUBLIC INTERNET does NOT reach the jobs API. The Cloudflare tunnel serves only
  playground -> originService https://localhost:443 (the gateway); six hours of
  cloudflared logs show no other dest. And boss-gcp has net.ipv4.ip_forward=0, so a
  WireGuard peer cannot hop through it into the cluster LAN. The back door is
  LAN-scoped, not internet-facing.

WHO IS ACTUALLY EXPOSED:
- Anything on the HOUSE LAN (192.168.1.0/24) — a guest laptop, a compromised IoT device.
  This is the real surface and the reason 'no guest could cause real issues' is not true
  in the general sense, even though it is true for a guest on playground.
- Anything on the CLUSTER VLAN (10.20.0.0/24).
- boss-gcp itself, which has a working route (confirmed 200) — so a boss-gcp compromise
  is a jobs-API-admin compromise. boss-gcp is a public GCP VM with SSH.

IMPORTANT LIMIT ON THE MACHINE TOKEN as a fix: it authenticates that a caller is a
legitimate MACHINE, not that x-boss-user is who they say. Any component holding the shared
token can still impersonate any user in the header. It stops LAN OUTSIDERS from writing;
it does not make x-boss-user trustworthy. And in phase 1, READS stay open even with the
token set — data disclosure from the LAN remains until a phase 2 that has not been
designed. The token is a mitigation, not the architectural fix.

THE TWO FIXES, in order of correctness:

(1) RESTRICT NETWORK REACH — the fix SECURITY.md actually prescribes. The jobs API should
    not be a LoadBalancer+NodePort reachable from the house LAN; it should be a ClusterIP
    the gateway alone reaches, or firewalled to the gateway. The complication, and the
    reason this is a car and not a one-liner: operator tooling reaches the back door on
    purpose — /Users/david/bin/boss-api is pinned to 10.20.0.34:7900, and the conductor on
    boss-gcp uses it too. Those callers have to move to the gateway (with real auth) or a
    firewalled path before the LoadBalancer can go.

(2) TURN ON BOSS_MACHINE_TOKEN — the pragmatic mitigation, and David's to do (token admin).
    ACTIVATION ORDER MATTERS, because turning it on 401s every writer that lacks it:

Service-to-service calls assert their identity with a header, over unencrypted internal HTTP.
Anything that can reach the pod network can forge platform-admin.

THE PATTERN, at 8 sites CodeQL flagged on publish PR #236:
  crates/core/boss-gateway/src/passkey.rs:270   (cleartext transmission + SSRF)
  crates/tenants/boss-brewery-engine/src/prepare/tenant_data.rs:564,593,622,667,733
The shape is the same everywhere - build an internal URL with format!, attach
  x-boss-user: {"id":"automation:gateway","role":"platform-admin"}
and send it over http. passkey.rs is explicit about why: boss-people's webauthn storage
requires a platform-admin caller because its paths are also browser-reachable through the
/api/people proxy, so it cannot trust callers by position. This header is how the ceremony
passes that gate.

WHY IT IS NOT AN EMERGENCY. The gateway strips actor headers at the edge, so an external
caller cannot inject one; the traffic is inside the cluster; and every service is on the pod
network already. CodeQL's "SSRF" label is weak here - the URL is built from a configured
api_base and a constant path, not from request data.

WHY IT IS STILL WORTH A DECISION. The control is positional: the header is trusted because of
WHERE it arrives from, and the only thing enforcing that is the edge strip. There is no
cryptographic binding between the claim "I am automation:gateway with platform-admin" and the
sender. Any workload that lands on the pod network - a compromised sidecar, a misconfigured
NetworkPolicy, a debug pod - can mint that header and get platform-admin against boss-people.
The blast radius is the whole people/webauthn surface.

OPTIONS, none of which I should pick unilaterally:
  (a) Accept and document. Record it as a deliberate trust boundary with the edge strip named
      as its control, and add a test that the strip actually happens (today that is prose).
  (b) Bind the claim. Sign the internal identity - a short-lived token or mTLS between
      services - so the header is evidence rather than an assertion.
  (c) Narrow the surface. Give the gateway a dedicated credential for boss-people's webauthn
      paths instead of a general platform-admin identity, so a forged header buys less.
(a) is cheap and honest; (b) is the real fix and is a substantial piece of work; (c) is a
middle path that reduces blast radius without changing transport.

PROVENANCE: found by CodeQL on the first publish PR in a fortnight, not by any gate - the
forge CI has no security scanning at all (ffc2c00c). Of that run's 46 alerts, 34 were test
fixtures and 3 were false positives I verified individually; this pattern is the only real
finding, and passkey.rs is NEW code written since 2026-08-12, so it was authored and proven in
prod without anything asking this question.

infra/gate-runner/run.sh picks the step it reports its verdict onto like this:

    [s["id"] for s in j["steps"] if "Record" in (s.get("title") or "")][0]

That is a match on HUMAN PROSE in a registry row. The live `gate-run v2` spec names that
step "Record the receipt", so it works today — by coincidence of wording, not by contract.

TWO WAYS IT BREAKS, BOTH SILENT UNTIL LATE:
  - Zero matches: `[0]` raises IndexError inside the runner. That happens AFTER the gate
    has run, so the cost is a full gate (~11-40 min of cluster time) that cannot report
    what it found.
  - Two matches: it reports onto whichever the API happened to order first, with no error
    at all.

Renaming that step in the workflow registry is an ordinary editorial act — protocols are
data and we edit them freely and on purpose. Nothing anywhere would flag it. The step title
is a fact that lives in two places (CLAUDE.md 9a) with neither a collapse nor a pin.

THE COLLAPSE, NOT A PIN. 9a says prefer collapsing, and here it is available: select by the
step's stable KEY ("record-verdict") rather than its rendered title. That requires the
materialized step JSON to expose the spec key — check whether it does; if not, exposing it
is the smaller and more generally useful change, because every other consumer that wants to
find a step by identity has the same problem.

A pin was drafted and deliberately discarded: it can only compare run.sh against a workflow
row in the repo, and `gate-run` is not in the repo at all — it exists solely as registry
data on the deployment. That is the correct place for a protocol to live, and it is exactly
why a repo-side test cannot guard this. The selector has to stop depending on prose.

metadata.body:
`boss train cancel` cannot close a PR on the forge, so every manual cancel leaves a
half-cancelled train: cars released, `cancelled` terminal never completed, PR still open,
train branch never deleted.

REPRODUCED TWICE, 2026-08-27, cancelling train e1de28a3 (PR 123):

  conductor: released car b10b3b52 back to the dock
  conductor: released car 0a3d2138 back to the dock
  conductor: released car 10e32168 back to the dock
  conductor: cancel: no CI runs were still active
  Error: gh pr close http://10.20.0.15:3000/david/boss/pulls/123: rc=1
  none of the git remotes configured for this repository point to a known GitHub host.

The car release happens BEFORE the PR close, so the destructive half succeeds and the
bookkeeping half fails. The train job stays `open` with `cancelled` pending and `merged`
ready, which is a train that has no cars and still advertises a merge step.

ROOT CAUSE: the cancel verb shells out to `gh pr close`. Since the forge cutover the
conductor clone's remotes point at http://10.20.0.15:3000/david/boss, and `gh` only
speaks to GitHub hosts, so the call cannot succeed by construction. It is not a
misconfiguration to fix on the box - the wrong tool is being invoked.

WHY IT HAS NOT BEEN NOTICED: the AUTOMATIC stall-based cancel works fine and completes
its terminal properly - train a960c89a auto-cancelled cleanly earlier the same day with
reason 'CI red and no progress for 6h'. So the two paths disagree: the automatic path
uses the Forgejo adapter, the manual verb uses `gh`. Manual cancels are rare, and their
most visible effect (cars returning to the dock) succeeds, so the failure reads as noise
at the end of a command that appeared to work.

A SECOND, EARLIER FAILURE MODE on the same command, worth fixing at the same time: run
from outside the conductor clone it dies with `failed to run git: fatal: not a git
repository` - also after releasing the cars. So there are two ways to half-cancel a
train, and both leave the same inconsistent state.

FIX: route the PR close through the same ForgejoForge adapter the automatic path uses,
and do the bookkeeping in an order where the irreversible step (releasing cars) is not
taken until the reversible ones have succeeded - or make the whole verb resumable, so
re-running it finishes what the first attempt started rather than re-releasing cars that
are already at the dock (it currently re-logs 'released car X back to the dock' for cars
that were already released, which is misleading).

EVIDENCE: train e1de28a3 is, at time of filing, open with cars=0, cancelled pending, and
PR 123 open with a red verdict. I deliberately did NOT hand-complete the terminal, so the
state is preserved for inspection and to let the stall sentinel demonstrate whether it
recovers it unaided.
metadata.correction_2026_08_27:
I MISATTRIBUTED THE ROOT CAUSE. This packet says `boss train cancel` 'shells out to gh pr close' and therefore 'cannot close a forge PR by construction'. That is wrong. The CLI selects its forge adapter from environment the systemd unit supplies and my ad-hoc invocation did not:
  BOSS_TRAIN_FORGE=forgejo, BOSS_TRAIN_FORGE_URL=http://10.20.0.15:3000,
  BOSS_TRAIN_FORGE_REPO=david/boss, BOSS_TRAIN_FORGE_TOKEN_FILE=/etc/boss-train/forge.token,
  BOSS_TRAIN_DEPLOY_REMOTE=forge, BOSS_JOBS_URL=http://10.20.0.34:7900
Without BOSS_TRAIN_FORGE the CLI falls back to gh/GitHub, which is why it tried `gh pr close http://10.20.0.15:3000/...`. Proven by re-running `boss train board` with that env present: it opened PR 125 on the forge cleanly (train af80597c). The automatic path was never broken - it always had the env - and my 'the two paths disagree' explanation was an artefact of comparing a correctly-configured service against an incorrectly-configured shell. The evidence I cited (an open PR, a train stuck with `cancelled` pending) was real; the cause I inferred from it was not.
TWO REAL DEFECTS SURVIVE THE CORRECTION, and they are why this packet stays open.
(1) ORDERING. The cars are released BEFORE the PR close is attempted, so any failure in the later step leaves the irreversible half done and the bookkeeping half undone: train open, `cancelled` pending, PR open, cars at the dock. That is true whatever caused the failure, and it is what produced two half-cancelled trains today (e1de28a3 and, from a failed board, 99ea7743). Do the reversible work first, or make the verb resumable so a second run finishes what the first started rather than re-logging 'released car X' for cars already released.
(2) THE VERB DOES NOT SAY IT IS MISCONFIGURED. preflight already refuses on a foreign-uid clone and on unreachable remotes - it is exactly the right place to assert 'a forge is configured' - but with BOSS_TRAIN_FORGE unset the command sails past preflight and only fails after it has changed state. A one-line preflight check would have turned my mistake into a refusal instead of a half-cancelled train.
TITLE IS NOW WRONG and should be re-read as: 'boss train cancel does its destructive half before its reversible half, and does not preflight its forge configuration'.
